fundmental_1.title: Synthetic Aperture Radar
fundmental_1.intro: The azimuth resolution of conventional real aperture radar depends on the dimension of the antenna and on the distance from the target. To achieve very high resolution in azimuth
fundmental_1.content: The azimuth resolution of conventional real aperture radar depends on the dimension of the antenna and on the distance from the target. To achieve very high resolution in azimuth, a very narrow beam is required. To get a very narrow beam, extremely long physical antenna is necessary. It is very difficult to build an antenna of several kilometers in length and operate from space. Therefore, Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) was developed to overcome the limitation of keeping long antenna in space. SAR systems use an antenna of much smaller physical dimensions, which sends pulses from different positions as the platform advances, simulating a synthetic aperture by integrating the pulse echoes into a composite signal. Aperture means the opening used to collect the reflected energy that is used to form an image. In the case of a camera, this would be the shutter opening, for radar it is the antenna. SAR can provide better resolution than conventional real aperture radars. By proper post processing important information can be extracted from the high resolution images acquired by SAR. The advantage of using Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) is that the spatial resolution is independent of platform altitude. Therefore, fine resolution can be achieved. Generally images are acquired in strips as the sensor moves along its flight path. These strips are called as swaths (the area illuminated by the antenna which is elongated and elliptical in shape). To separate the objects in the range direction (perpendicular to flight path), radar echoes are separated using the time delay between echoes that are backscattered from the different scatterers. To separate the objects in azimuth direction (parallel to the flight path) Doppler frequency is used. Since time delay and Doppler frequency is used to separate the objects on the Earth surface, the resolution is independent of the distance between the radar and the target.

fundament_4.title: Polarimetric Synthetic Aperture Radar (PolSAR)
fundament_4.intro: Polarimetric Synthetic Aperture Radar (PolSAR) revolutionized radar remote sensing by providing detailed insights into the characteristics of objects and terrain through their scattering properties.
fundament_4.content: In comparison with traditional systems that were based on single-polarization information, the main feature of PolSAR is its capability to both transmit and receive microwave signals in multiple polarizations, such as vertical (V), horizontal (H), and cross-polarizations (HV or VH). This technology allows PolSAR to gain the total polarimetric scattering information, namely the amplitude and the phase of the received signal, to conduct a detailed analysis of the scattering process. As a result, PolSAR improves the differentiation capability between various target types, such as vegetation, man-made structures, and natural features, making it a versatile tool for applications in agriculture, forestry, and land cover classification. With the launch of dedicated PolSAR satellites, the technology has become more accessible and widespread, enabling global monitoring and comprehensive Earth observation. Ongoing research continues to refine PolSAR processing techniques, enhancing its capabilities in fields like terrain analysis, environmental assessment, and target recognition. As it evolves, PolSAR remains at the forefront of radar remote sensing, providing a valuable perspective on our planet's dynamic features and complex environments.

fundament_5.title: Polarization Correlation
fundament_5.intro: Polarization correlation in polarimetry explains the degree of correlation or relation between the polarization states of the radar waves.
fundament_5.content: Within the context of Polarimetric Synthetic Aperture Radar (PolSAR), polarization correlation is a fundamental concept explaining the relations among different combinations of polarization states. It is divided into two main forms: co-polarization and cross-polarization. Co-polarization refers to the relationship between horizontal (H) and vertical (V) polarization states of the radar waves. In PolSAR, HH (horizontal transmit and horizontal receive) and VV (vertical transmit and vertical receive) are co-polarized signals. High co-polarization indicates that radar waves maintain a strong correlation in their polarization states. Cross-polarization refers to the correlation between horizontal transmission and vertical reception (HV) or between vertical transmission and horizontal reception (VH). These channels represent cross-polarized signals. Low cross-polarization suggests that the polarization states are weakly correlated, which is often indicative of surface or volume scattering.

fundment_10.title: Interferometry
fundment_10.intro: Interferometry is a remote sensing technique using radar imagery to measure surface deformation or topography through the interpretation of phase differences between two or more radar images of the same scene.
fundment_10.content: The phase of a radar signal contains information about the distance between the radar sensor and the target surface. An interferogram results from comparing the phase values generated from two radar signals: the interferogram exhibits a change in distance from the sensor to the ground for each of its corresponding images. This phase difference responds very sensitively to any kind of slight displacement resulting from earthquakes, landslides, or subsidence as well as to variations in elevation. Factors that contribute to the quality of phase information include wavelength, baseline distance (the separation between the sensor positions), and the surface roughness. Interferometry is highly sensitive, capable of measuring minute changes on Earth's surface on the order of millimeters, making it a powerful tool for studying Earth's dynamics.
